study.title: Revelation 22 The End of Vision and the Final Call for Grace
study.overview: Revelation 22 encloses the vision with images of total restoration: the river of life, the tree of life, the absence of curse, the immediate presence of God and the Lamb, and the continuous light of the Lord himself. The chapter also confirms the reliability of the prophecy, calls obedience, rejects worship to any created being, announces the closeness of fulfillment and ends with an open invitation to spiritual thirst and a final blessing of grace. The tone is at the same time comforting and solemn: there is promise to the believers and to the unfaithful.

outline.title: The city as a restored paradise
outline.explanation: John sees the water of life, the tree of life and the elimination of the curse. The scene describes full communion with God, uninterrupted service, vision of his face and reign without night, without shadow and no need for created light.

outline.title: Prophecy Is True and Demands Immediate Response
outline.explanation: The angel confirms that the words are faithful and that the time is near. John is corrected when he tries to worship the angel, and receives the command not to seal the prophecy, for the judgment and moral condition of each person walk for his confirmation.

outline.title: Christ speaks, invites and seals the book with grace
outline.explanation: Jesus presents himself as Alpha and Omega, promises retribution according to works, defines who enters the city and who is left outside, calls the thirsty to drink for free, warns against changing the prophecy and concludes with the promise of his coming and the blessing of grace.

study.context: The chapter works as a closure of both the vision of the new Jerusalem and the whole book. The notes highlight the parallel with the paradise of the beginning of Scripture and with already known prophetic images, especially those of Ezekiel, where there are rivers and fruit trees. There are also echoes of the language of blessing, invitation and warning found in other parts of the Bible. The picture is eschatological: it describes not only inner comfort, but the final destiny of the people of God and the outcome of history under the rule of God and the Lamb.
study.theology: Chapter theology is deeply centered on God, the Lamb and the consummation of salvation. The new creation appears as a restoration of access to life that sin had closed: the tree of life is given again free of charge, the curse is removed, and the presence of God is not only mediated, but contemplated. The river of life suggests continuous provision that comes from the throne, that is, life received from God and not produced by the human being. The chapter also unites promise and responsibility: bliss is linked to obedience, and the warning against adding or taking words from prophecy shows that the revelation of God is sufficient and holy. The exclusion of the wicked is not presented as secondary detail, but as a real contrast to the entry of those who wash their lives into God's government. Finally, the grace of Christ closes the book: Christian hope does not end in fear, but in the presence and coming of the Lord Jesus.

scholarViews.insight: The water of life is presented as a divine provision that springs from the throne of God and the Lamb, in parallel with the images of provision and restoration already known in the Scriptures.
The vision of the new Jerusalem is understood as a restored paradise, opposed to Eden lost by Adam, now renewed by the second Adam.
The tree of life is linked to Eden and the images of Ezekiel, suggesting continuous and abundant provision of life for the inhabitants of the city.

questions: What changes in the way of living when the final hope is the presence of God and the Lamb, and not just the relief of present sufferings?
In what practical ways does the call not to add or take away from the words of prophecy confronts our attitudes before the Bible today?
To whom the invitation of Jesus in Revelation 22:17 leads us to look more urgently: to the believers, to the thirsty, or to those who are outside?
study.practice: Long live this chapter as hope and warning at the same time. Cultivate a concrete attachment to the Word: read it with reverence, without twisting its sense to adjust to personal preferences. Respond to Christ's invitation with faith and real thirst, seeking in him the water of life. Also practice exclusive worship of God, refusing any form of devotion that displaces Christ from the center. In the daily routine, this can mean sincere prayer, visible obedience and clear testimony that our hope is at the coming of the Lord Jesus.
study.uncertainty: The available notes of Matthew Henry came partially summarized in some excerpts, so the synthesis was built only with the content provided. It is also not possible to accurately determine, from the notes, all the details of the variant readings mentioned by Adam Clarke, so conclusions have been avoided beyond what is explicitly indicated.
